strengths: Introduces a timely and clearly motivated benchmark for paper-code discrepancy detection, a genuinely important QA problem for computational science and NLP/AI reproducibility.
The task definition is thoughtful: the paper distinguishes meaningful scientific discrepancies from ordinary bugs, configurable hyperparameters, and minor engineering details.

Dataset construction combines realistic sources from GitHub issues and reproducibility reports with synthetic code modifications, yielding broader domain coverage than the small real subset alone would allow.

The paper provides useful analyses by discrepancy origin, type, category, prompt length, publication year, and programming language, which makes the benchmark more informative than a single leaderboard.
Evaluation covers a broad set of proprietary and open models, and the code-only ablation is a good sanity check showing that the paper context matters.
The authors make several reproducibility-minded choices, including versioning papers/code around the time discrepancies were reported and documenting prompts and model configurations in the appendix.
weaknesses: The main real-world ground truth is quite small: only 81 discrepancies from 67 papers. This limits confidence in broad claims about real-world paper-code QA, especially outside CS/AI.

The pipeline depends heavily on LLMs at multiple crucial stages: candidate extraction, final validation/phrasing, synthetic discrepancy generation, and LLM-as-judge evaluation. Manual filtering is mentioned, but the paper gives limited detail on annotator expertise, annotation protocol, disagreement resolution, or inter-annotator reliability.

The synthetic subset is useful but not fully validated as a proxy for real discrepancies. The reported real-vs-synthetic performance correlation mostly supports model ranking consistency, not necessarily that synthetic discrepancies match the distribution, difficulty, or semantics of naturally occurring discrepancies.

Evaluation emphasizes recall against known annotations, but the ground truth is incomplete. The small precision analysis on 12 NLP papers is valuable, yet too limited to fully characterize false positives or support general deployment conclusions.
Using GPT-OSS 20B as judge while also evaluating GPT-OSS models introduces possible self-preference bias; the authors acknowledge this, but it still affects confidence in reported scores.

Input truncation removes whole code files from the end when repositories exceed context limits. This can silently remove the relevant evidence for some discrepancies and may confound model comparisons across different context windows.

The benchmark may be vulnerable to contamination because many papers and repositories are public and within model pretraining cutoffs; the publication-year analysis is suggestive but not a complete contamination control.

Some claims are phrased strongly relative to the evidence, particularly around synthetic data being a reliable proxy and SCICOQA enabling assurance for future AI-scientist workflows. The empirical contribution is sound, but the broader claims should be more carefully qualified.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: checking whether scientific code faithfully implements the corresponding paper is directly relevant to reproducibility, peer review, and NLP/code-understanding evaluation.

The discrepancy taxonomy is sensible and the task formulation is clearer than many prior error-detection benchmarks, distinguishing meaningful paper-code mismatches from ordinary bugs or configurable hyperparameter differences.
The real-world sources, GitHub issues and reproducibility reports, are appropriate starting points, and the examples shown are concrete and compelling.
The paper evaluates a broad set of current proprietary and open models and includes useful analyses by discrepancy type, source, prompt length, publication year, and code-only ablation.
weaknesses: The central benchmark is not sufficiently well validated. Only 81 real discrepancies are included, and the paper itself shows substantial label incompleteness: in a small 12-paper NLP subset, model outputs reveal many additional valid discrepancies not in the ground truth. This seriously undermines the reported recall numbers and the claim that the dataset can support reliable evaluation.

The methodology relies heavily on LLMs for discovery, verification, phrasing, synthetic generation, and evaluation. GPT-5 is used to validate and phrase ground-truth discrepancies and also appears as a benchmarked system, while GPT-OSS is used as judge and also as a tested model family. These circular dependencies create bias risks that are not adequately controlled.

The synthetic data, which constitutes the overwhelming majority of the dataset, is generated by GPT-5 modifications rather than observed real discrepancies. The evidence that it is a valid proxy is weak: a high correlation in model rankings does not establish that synthetic errors match the distribution, difficulty, or semantics of real paper-code discrepancies.

Human annotation details are under-specified. The paper does not report multiple annotators, adjudication, inter-annotator agreement, annotation guidelines in sufficient operational detail, or systematic auditing of rejected candidates. For a dataset paper, this is a major reproducibility and validity gap.

The evaluation protocol is fragile. Matching predictions to references via an LLM judge validated on only 20 discrepancies and top-3 embedding-filtered candidates is too small and potentially biased for a benchmark whose outputs are open-ended and semantically subtle.

The reported results are difficult to interpret because the metric is effectively reference-discrepancy recall over an incomplete set, while valid unannotated predictions are common. Precision is analyzed only on 12 NLP papers, so the main benchmark does not provide a reliable overall picture of model quality.

Input construction introduces confounds: code is truncated by dropping files from the end when context is exceeded, which may remove relevant evidence differently across repositories and models. The paper does not sufficiently analyze how often ground-truth evidence is truncated or whether model failures are due to missing context.

Claims about contamination and publication-year effects are speculative. Differences by year could reflect repository size, domain, code maturity, or discrepancy type, and the paper does not isolate these factors.

Reproducibility remains uncertain despite the stated release. The experiments depend on commercial APIs, OCR conversion, repository snapshots, exact prompts, long-context truncation, and LLM judging; more precise artifacts and auditing would be needed for independent replication.

Overall, the task is valuable, but the current evidence does not support the paper’s stronger claims about benchmark reliability or synthetic-data validity. The work needs substantial revision before it can be considered a sound Findings contribution.

strengths: SCICOQA targets an important and under-served problem: verifying semantic alignment between scientific papers and released code. This is highly relevant to NLP/CL given current interest in automated reviewing, scientific agents, long-context reasoning, and reproducibility.

The task formulation is clear and useful. The paper gives a concrete discrepancy definition, separates differences, paper omissions, and code omissions, and distinguishes scientific mismatches from ordinary bugs or configurable hyperparameter choices.

The dataset construction is thoughtfully sourced: real discrepancies come from GitHub issues and reproducibility reports, while synthetic examples broaden coverage beyond AI/CS into other computational science domains. The use of versioned papers and repositories is a strong reproducibility choice.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering 21 proprietary and open-weight models, multiple model families, code-only ablations, context-length analysis, publication-year analysis, and discrepancy-type analysis. The results support the central claim that current LLMs have insufficient recall for autonomous paper-code QA.

The authors include useful validation beyond headline recall: LLM-judge agreement is checked against human annotations, unlabeled model predictions are manually analyzed for precision on a subset, and a pooled-ground-truth analysis confirms that many valid discrepancies remain hard to find.

The paper is generally well written, well motivated, and provides prompts, model versions, preprocessing details, and examples, which makes the contribution relatively transparent and likely reusable.
weaknesses: The real-world portion is quite small: only 81 discrepancies from 67 papers. This is understandable given the difficulty of collection, but it limits confidence in conclusions about real-world prevalence, domain coverage, and fine-grained breakdowns by discrepancy type or source.

The pipeline depends heavily on GPT-5 for extracting, validating, phrasing, and generating discrepancies. This is practical, but it raises concerns about hidden model biases, missed valid examples, and possible circularity when evaluating later LLMs on data partly created or standardized by a very strong LLM.

Human validation is present but not described in enough detail. The paper would be stronger with clearer annotation protocol information: number and expertise of annotators, whether multiple annotators checked each item, adjudication procedure, and inter-annotator agreement for real discrepancies and labels.

The synthetic data is useful but not fully validated as a substitute for real discrepancies. The high real/synthetic performance correlation mainly shows similar model ranking, not necessarily that synthetic discrepancies match the distribution, subtlety, or evidential ambiguity of naturally occurring paper-code mismatches.

Evaluation relies on an LLM judge and reports primarily recall against an incomplete ground truth. The authors do analyze precision on a subset, but the main benchmark scores may still be sensitive to judge behavior, verbosity of model predictions, and unannotated true positives.

The context-processing strategy truncates whole files from the end of the code prompt when repositories exceed context limits. This is reproducible, but may introduce arbitrary repository-order effects and does not reflect stronger retrieval-based or agentic QA systems that could inspect code selectively.

Some claims are slightly stronger than the evidence warrants. For example, interpreting worse performance on newer papers as evidence of pretraining contamination is plausible, but alternative explanations such as repository complexity, domain mix, or paper style are not fully ruled out.

The work is sound and valuable, but its main novelty is primarily benchmark construction rather than a new modeling method or deep analysis of discrepancy causes. Together with the small real set and LLM-heavy pipeline, this makes it closer to borderline main-conference than a clear top-tier acceptance.
